draft.title: The innate immune response
card: The innate immune response starts within minutes to hours of a pathogen getting past the barriers. It is non-specific: it reacts the same way to many different pathogens and does not need to have met them before.
Inflammation

Damaged cells and mast cells release chemicals such as histamine. Blood vessels widen and become leakier, so more fluid and white blood cells reach the site. This causes redness, heat, swelling and pain.
Phagocytes and NK cells

Phagocytes, such as neutrophils and macrophages, engulf and digest pathogens. Natural killer (NK) cells destroy body cells that are infected by viruses or have become cancerous, by triggering them to die.
Complement proteins
Complement proteins circulate in the blood. When activated, they can coat pathogens so phagocytes engulf them more easily, and some can make holes in pathogen membranes.
draft.remember: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific: inflammation brings cells in, and phagocytes, NK cells and complement proteins attack.

a.q: A student says the innate response is non-specific. What does this mean?
opts: It acts in a similar way against many different pathogens
It only acts on pathogens the body has met before
It only works against one type of pathogen at a time
It is activated only after antibodies have been made
a.why: Innate responses do not depend on recognising one particular pathogen or on earlier exposure, so they act in a similar way against many. The option about previous meetings describes a response that depends on memory, which the card does not attribute to innate immunity.
a.clue: Think about whether the response needs to have met the pathogen before.

b.q: Liam gets a splinter in his finger. Within an hour the area is red, warm and swollen. What is the main reason the area becomes swollen?
opts: Blood vessels become leakier, so fluid enters the tissue
NK cells release fluid as they destroy the splinter
Complement proteins swell as they coat the splinter
Phagocytes multiply and fill the space inside the cells
b.why: Chemicals such as histamine widen blood vessels and make them leakier, so fluid and white blood cells move into the tissue and cause swelling. NK cells target infected or cancerous body cells, not splinters, so they are not the cause of the swelling.
b.clue: Which change in blood vessels lets fluid reach the injured tissue?

a.best: It acts in a similar way against many different pathogens

b.best: Blood vessels become leakier, so fluid enters the tissue
